source: Summaries of Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) guidance, ico.org.uk

records.title: Cost of compliance exceeds the appropriate limit
records.test: An authority does not have to comply if it estimates that determining whether it holds the information, and locating, retrieving and extracting it, would exceed the appropriate limit: £450 for local authorities, calculated at £25 per hour (18 hours).
key_points: Time spent considering exemptions or redacting cannot be counted.
The estimate must be reasonable and based on evidence.
Under the section 16 duty to advise and assist, the authority should explain how the request could be narrowed to fall within the limit.
Typical triggers are requests for all emails or all documents on a topic over many years, or information that would need searching manually across many files.

records.title: Vexatious and repeated requests
records.test: Section 14(1): an authority does not have to comply with a vexatious request, one likely to cause a disproportionate or unjustified level of disruption, irritation or distress. Section 14(2): it need not comply with a request identical or substantially similar to a previous request from the same person unless a reasonable interval has passed.
key_points: The focus is on the request, not the requester, although the history and context can be taken into account.
Abusive or threatening language, unreasonable persistence and lack of serious purpose are indicators.
There is no public interest test.

records.title: Information reasonably accessible to the applicant by other means
records.test: Absolute exemption for information already reasonably accessible to the requester, for example published on the authority's website or through its publication scheme.
key_points: Give a precise link or directions so the requester can find the information without difficulty.
The published information must actually answer the request, including the time period asked for. If it only partly answers it, the rest must be dealt with.
Information that is only available on request is not reasonably accessible.

records.title: Information intended for future publication
records.test: Qualified exemption where, at the time of the request, the authority has a settled intention to publish the information at a future date and it is reasonable to withhold it until then.
key_points: The intention to publish must exist when the request is received.
A public interest test applies.
Common examples are reports, statistics and accounts that are due to be published.

records.title: Law enforcement
records.test: Qualified exemption where disclosure would, or would be likely to, prejudice the prevention or detection of crime, the apprehension or prosecution of offenders, or the authority's regulatory and enforcement functions.
key_points: Councils often consider it for CCTV camera locations, fraud detection methods, lists of empty properties and cyber security details.
The prejudice must be real and significant, and a public interest test applies.

records.title: Personal information
records.test: Section 40(1): the requester's own personal data is absolutely exempt and handled as a subject access request. Section 40(2): third-party personal data is exempt if disclosure would breach the data protection principles, usually assessed through the legitimate interests test.
key_points: Senior staff in public-facing roles have a greater expectation that their names, roles and salary bands may be disclosed than junior staff.
Exact salaries of named junior employees, sickness records, disciplinary details and information about service users are normally withheld.
Small numbers in statistics can identify individuals. Councils often suppress figures below five.
Information about people who have died is not personal data, but other exemptions such as s41 may apply.

records.title: Information provided in confidence
records.test: Absolute exemption for information obtained from another person where disclosure would be an actionable breach of confidence.
key_points: The information must have come from a third party, have the necessary quality of confidence and have been given in circumstances creating an obligation of confidence.
The terms of a contract agreed between the authority and a supplier are not usually treated as obtained from another person.

records.title: Legal professional privilege
records.test: Qualified exemption for information covered by legal professional privilege, such as confidential legal advice to the authority.
key_points: There is a strong inherent public interest in protecting legal privilege.

records.title: Commercial interests
records.test: Section 43(2): qualified exemption where disclosure would, or would be likely to, prejudice the commercial interests of any person, including the authority itself.
key_points: Commonly considered for contract pricing, unit rates, tender bids and supplier information.
The prejudice must be specific and evidenced. It is usually weaker once a procurement has finished.
The public interest in transparency of public spending often favours disclosing contract values.
